title: Iran Just Claimed Ownership of the World's Most Important Shipping Lane. India Has 200,000 Reasons to Worry.
excerpt: A second tanker was hit on Saturday as Tehran demands ships get Iranian permits to cross the Strait of Hormuz, and Washington warns 'violence will be met with violence.' For India, whose seafarers and oil supply depend on the strait, the ceasefire that was supposed to fix everything is falling apart.
body:
The ceasefire was nine days old when it died.

On Saturday morning, a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz reported being struck by a projectile, sustaining damage to its bridge. All crew were reported safe. Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency confirmed the attack, and the Joint Maritime Information Center — run by a coalition of navies protecting shipping — raised its security threat level in the strait.

It was the second commercial vessel hit in three days, following Thursday's drone strike on the Singapore-flagged cargo ship *Ever Lovely*, which prompted overnight US air strikes on Iranian missile and drone storage locations and coastal radar sites at the port city of Sirik.

## Iran's New Red Line

But the deeper story is not about any single strike. It is about what Iran is now demanding: control of who gets to cross the strait.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps issued a public warning that all ships must coordinate with Iranian authorities and use an Iranian-approved traffic separation scheme. Iranian state television reported that the Guards had fired "warning shots" at unspecified ships attempting to pass through routes not approved by Iran, and that other ships were now seeking Iranian permits before attempting the crossing.

Ebrahim Azizi, head of Iran's parliamentary national security committee, was explicit on Saturday: "The Strait of Hormuz is governed by Iran. Respect the rules." He added: "Do not mistake control for escalation."

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi went further, saying "safe passage through the strait cannot be guaranteed under ambiguous arrangements, parallel routes or decision-making that does not take Iran's role as a coastal state into account."

The message to the world was unmistakable: Iran intends to charge a toll — in compliance, if not in cash — for every barrel of oil that leaves the Persian Gulf.

## The American Response

Washington has promoted a southern shipping lane along the coast of Oman, established jointly by Oman and the International Maritime Organization. US Central Command said it was providing "safe passage coordination and support" to commercial vessels using that route.

Vice President JD Vance, now President Trump's chief negotiator on the conflict, responded on X with a blunt warning: "Iran signed a ceasefire agreement. We have honored it. If they have disagreements about how the MOU is being applied, they can pick up the phone. But violence will be met with violence."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, wrapping up a tour of the Gulf, issued a joint statement with the Gulf Cooperation Council calling for "free, unconditional, and unrestricted navigation" without tolls or attempts to assert control.

Iran's foreign ministry shot back that the strait should be governed jointly by Iran and Oman — conspicuously excluding the United States. Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran's supreme leader, warned Washington's Gulf allies that "their survival depended on Tehran's tolerance."

## What This Means for India

India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, and before the war, a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz. India has more than 200,000 seafarers working on international commercial vessels, thousands of whom transit the strait regularly.

Three Indian seafarers have already died in attacks on commercial ships during the conflict. India lodged a strong protest with the United States after the attack on the vessel MT Settebello and summoned the US Charge d'Affaires to convey that "the welfare of our seafaring community is very important, and the attacks that are happening must stop."

The ceasefire, signed on June 18, was supposed to change the calculus. Oil prices had tumbled close to pre-war levels as tankers began exiting the Gulf. Saudi Aramco resumed crude loadings at its Ras Tanura terminal — the world's biggest oil port — after a nearly four-month halt. Fertilizer shipments picked up too.

But Iran's new posture threatens to reverse all of that. If ships must seek Iranian permits, insurance rates will climb. If tankers are attacked for using the Omani route, some operators will simply stay away. And if the strait becomes a toll road under Iranian management, every barrel India imports from the Gulf will carry a geopolitical surcharge.

For India, the worst outcome is not another weekend of strikes. It is a permanent arrangement in which Tehran controls the chokepoint that feeds India's refineries, its factories, and its 1.4 billion people — and can turn it off whenever it wants.

The ceasefire was supposed to reopen the world's most important waterway. Instead, it may have handed Iran the key to lock it.
